skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: pptx
skills.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.

skills.name: ast-consistency
skills.description: AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged.

skills.name: body-removal
skills.description: Remove function bodies from Rust/Verus source files to produce signature-only views. Used before the view-design phase to prevent implementation anchoring.

skills.name: bug-reporting
skills.description: Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug.

skills.name: caller-analysis
skills.description: Analyze callers of a Rust module to understand usage expectations for Verus verification. Produces a caller-perspective analysis covering all functions with their visibility and call relationships.

skills.name: crate-analysis
skills.description: Principles for verification order in multi-file Rust crates. Verify leaf modules first so downstream modules can reference upstream specs directly. The pipeline tool handles ordering automatically.

skills.name: proof-extraction
skills.description: Extract large inline proof blocks from exec code into named lemmas in .proof.rs. Use when polishing verified code to improve readability and proof organization.

skills.name: proof-minimization
skills.description: Remove redundant proof artifacts (assertions, lemmas, hints, dead code) without weakening guarantees. Use when polishing verified code to reduce verbosity.

skills.name: property-analysis
skills.description: How to analyze source code and identify verification properties — the WHAT of verification. Covers module understanding, property discovery across four dimensions (functional correctness, safety, liveness, structural consistency), and quality review. Use this skill when deciding what to verify for a new module, writing property_analysis.md, or updating global_properties.md.

skills.name: proving-guide
skills.description: Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures.

skills.name: review-methodology
skills.description: Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks.

skills.name: spec-completeness
skills.description: Detect specification incompleteness via nondeterminism checking. Given a Verus function spec, automatically determine whether the spec uniquely determines the output for each valid input. If not, use type-guided binary search to construct a concrete witness (input + two valid but different outputs). No LLM needed — pure SMT-based.

skills.name: spec-design
skills.description: How to write good Verus specs. Covers spec quality principles (anti-patterns, error paths), spec classification (internal, external-top, external-bottom trust boundaries), View abstraction design, and static vs dynamic enforcement. Use when writing or reviewing Verus specs.

skills.name: verus-constraints
skills.description: Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code.

skills.name: verus-setup
skills.description: Set up Verus formal verification infrastructure for a Rust project. Covers workspace-level config (vstd dependency, cfg flags, version pinning, Makefile, scripts) and per-crate config (metadata, cfg-gated includes, spec/proof stubs). Use this skill when preparing a repo or crate for Verus verification, adding make verify support, or integrating cheating detection into a build.

skills.name: verus-syntax
skills.description: Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example.

skills.name: view-design
skills.description: How to design a View type that represents abstract state from the caller's perspective. Input: caller analysis + property concepts. Must NOT see implementation code.

skills.name: customize-cloud-agent
skills.description: Skill for customizing the Copilot cloud agent (formerly known as Copilot coding agent) environment, including copilot-setup-steps.yml configuration, preinstalling tools and dependencies, runners, and settings.

result.content:
1. # Specification Review: cache
2. 
3. > Consolidated from independent reviews by claude-opus-4.6 and gpt-5.3-codex.
4. > Raw outputs: `review_r1.claude.md`, `review_r1.gpt.md`.
5. 
6. ## Checklist
7. ### Specification
8. - [x] Every in-scope exec function has requires/ensures
9. - [x] No tautological ensures (e.g., `Err(_) => true`)
10. - [ ] No subsumed ensures (derivable from inv() + other ensures)
11. - [ ] Error paths have meaningful ensures (match style: Ok => ..., Err => ...)
12. - [x] No assume_specification for workspace-internal code
13. - [x] vstd searched before any assume_specification
14. - [ ] Specs written for the caller (usable directly in caller proofs)
15. 
16. **Unchecked items:**
17. - **Subsumed ensures**: Every function (`new`, `get`, `put`, `remove`, `clear`)
18.   carries 3–5 ensures clauses that are strict unfoldings of the `== spec_*(…)`
19.   canonical clause. Since all spec transition functions are `pub open spec fn`,
20.   callers can unfold them directly. These clauses are redundant bloat.
21. - **Error paths**: `get` on miss is well-specified (`self@ == old(self)@`), but
22.   the hit path does not meaningfully constrain the return value — `result is Some`
23.   without any link to the cached value is effectively a one-sided spec.
24. - **Caller usability**: `CacheGuard::deref` and `CacheGuard::deref_mut` have
25.   **no specs at all**. Since these are the only way callers extract values from
26.   `get`, the specification chain is broken: callers cannot prove they receive
27.   the correct value.
28. 
29. ## Determinism Check
30. | Function | Result | Under-constrained aspect |
31. |---|---|---|
32. | `Cache::get` (return value) | INCOMPLETE | On hit: only `result is Some`. The value inside `CacheGuard` is entirely unconstrained — no View impl, no Deref spec. A conforming implementation could return arbitrary data. |
33. | `CacheGuard::deref` | INCOMPLETE | No spec at all. |
34. | `CacheGuard::deref_mut` | INCOMPLETE | No spec at all. |
35. 
36. All other functions (`new`, `put`, `remove`, `clear`, `evict`) are COMPLETE —
37. the `== spec_*(…)` clause fully determines the post-state and return value.
38. 
39. ## Caller Coverage Issues
40. | Function | Status | Notes |
41. |---|---|---|
42. | `Cache::get` | MISSING_SPEC | Return value unconstrained on hit. Caller expectation "guard dereferences to stored value" (caller analysis §CacheGuard::deref) is unverifiable. |
43. | `CacheGuard::deref` | MISSING_SPEC | No contract. This is the primary value-extraction interface. |
44. | `CacheGuard::deref_mut` | MISSING_SPEC | No contract. Mutation-through-guard behavior unmodeled. |
45. | `Cache::new` | SUBSUMED | 4 ensures clauses are unfoldings of `spec_new` (which is `open`). |
46. | `Cache::put` | SUBSUMED | Round-trip and zero-cap clauses derivable from `spec_put`. |
47. | `Cache::remove` | SUBSUMED | Key-absent no-op and key-not-present clauses derivable from `spec_remove`. |
48. | `Cache::clear` | SUBSUMED | Emptiness/order/capacity clauses derivable from `spec_clear`. |
49. 
50. ## Missing Properties
51. 1. **Get-value correctness (CRITICAL)** — The fundamental cache contract ("you
52.    get back what you put in") is unverifiable. `get` on hit says `result is Some`
53.    but never connects the `CacheGuard` to `old(self)@.contents[*key]`. The
54.    `spec_get` transition function returns `(CacheView, Option<V>)` and the
55.    `Option<V>` component is never referenced in the exec ensures.
56.    **Fix**: Either (a) add a View impl for `CacheGuard` mapping to `V` plus a
57.    spec on `Deref`, or (b) add an ensures clause directly on `get` such as
58.    `result matches Some(g) ==> *g == old(self)@.contents[*key]` (if Verus can
59.    express this through the external-body guard).
60. 
61. 2. **Guard mutation effect** — If a caller mutates through `DerefMut`, the
62.    cache entry should reflect the change. Currently unspecified. This is a
63.    known Verus limitation (`&mut` in struct fields) but should be documented
64.    in trust.md.
65. 
66. 3. **Counter overflow** — `self.counter` is `u64`, incremented on every `get`
67.    hit and `put`. The spec has no precondition guarding overflow. While 2⁶⁴
68.    operations is physically unreachable, a rigorous spec would either add
69.    `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` or document the trust assumption. The
70.    property analysis (BUG-1) identifies this; it should be recorded in
71.    trust.md.
72. 
73. ## Specs to Remove
74. - **`new`**: Remove `result@.inv()`, `result@.contents == Map::empty()`,
75.   `result@.capacity == capacity as nat`, `result@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`.
76.   All derivable from `result@ == spec_new(…)` (open spec).
77. - **`get` (hit)**: Remove `self@.contents == old(self)@.contents`,
78.   `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, `self@.inv()`.
79.   All derivable from `self@ == old(self)@.spec_get(*key).0`.
80. - **`put`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, put-get round-trip
81.   block, zero-capacity no-op block. All derivable from `self@ == spec_put(…)`.
82. - **`remove`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`,
83.   `!self@.contents.dom().contains(*key)`,
84.   `!old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> self@ == old(self)@`.
85.   All derivable from `self@ == spec_remove(…)`.
86. - **`clear`**: Remove `self@.contents == Map::empty()`,
87.   `self@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`, `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`.
88.   All derivable from `self@ == spec_clear()`.
89. 
90. **Caveat**: Keeping `self@.inv()` on each function is a reasonable ergonomic
91. choice — it saves callers from invoking invariant-preservation lemmas. The
92. field-level unfoldings, however, add pure maintenance burden.
93. 
94. ## Issues (highest priority first)
95. 
96. 1. **🔴 CRITICAL — `get` return value unspecified.** The ensures says
97.    `result is Some` on hit but never constrains what the `CacheGuard` provides.
98.    A conforming implementation could return any `V`. This defeats the fundamental
99.    purpose of the cache. The `spec_get` spec function computes the correct
100.    `Option<V>` but it is never connected to the exec return value.
101. 
102. 2. **🔴 CRITICAL — `CacheGuard::Deref`/`DerefMut` have no specs.** These are
103.    the only way callers access values from `get`. Without contracts, the
104.    specification chain from `put` → `get` → `*guard` is broken.
105. 
106. 3. **🟡 MODERATE — Pervasive subsumed clauses.** Every function carries 3–5
107.    ensures that merely unfold the canonical `== spec_*(…)` clause. This bloats
108.    the spec, increases maintenance burden, and risks divergence if spec functions
109.    are updated. Prune to `== spec_*(…)` + `inv()`.
110. 
111. 4. **🟡 MODERATE — Counter overflow unaddressed.** `u64` counter incremented
112.    without bounds checking. The property analysis identifies this (BUG-1) but
113.    it is not recorded in bugs.md or trust.md as a verification assumption.
114. 
115. 5. **🟢 MINOR — `inv()` redundant conjunct.** `lru_order.len() == contents.dom().len()`
116.    follows from `no_duplicates()` + `to_set() == dom()`. Acceptable as an SMT
117.    trigger / solver hint.
118. 
119. 6. **🟢 MINOR — No bugs.md file.** The property analysis identifies BUG-1
120.    (counter overflow) but no bugs.md exists to track it.
121. 
122. ## Result: FAIL
123. 
124. **Reason**: Two checklist items are unchecked:
125. 1. Subsumed ensures throughout all functions.
126. 2. `get` hit path does not meaningfully constrain the return value, and
127.    `CacheGuard::deref`/`deref_mut` lack specs entirely — callers cannot
128.    use the specification to verify correct data retrieval.
129. 
130. Both CRITICAL issues (items 1–2) must be resolved before the specification
131. can pass review.
132.

    known Verus limitation (`&mut` in struct fields) but should be documented
    in trust.md.
 
 3. **Counter overflow** — `self.counter` is `u64`, incremented on every `get`
    hit and `put`. The spec has no precondition guarding overflow. While 2⁶⁴
    operations is physically unreachable, a rigorous spec would either add
    `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` or document the trust assumption. The
    property analysis (BUG-1) identifies this; it should be recorded in
    trust.md.
 
 ## Specs to Remove
 - **`new`**: Remove `result@.inv()`, `result@.contents == Map::empty()`,
   `result@.capacity == capacity as nat`, `result@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`.
   All derivable from `result@ == spec_new(…)` (open spec).
 - **`get` (hit)**: Remove `self@.contents == old(self)@.contents`,
   `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, `self@.inv()`.
   All derivable from `self@ == old(self)@.spec_get(*key).0`.
 - **`put`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, put-get round-trip
   block, zero-capacity no-op block. All derivable from `self@ == spec_put(…)`.
 - **`remove`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`,
   `!self@.contents.dom().contains(*key)`,
   `!old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> self@ == old(self)@`.
   All derivable from `self@ == spec_remove(…)`.
 - **`clear`**: Remove `self@.contents == Map::empty()`,
   `self@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`, `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`.
   All derivable from `self@ == spec_clear()`.
 
 **Caveat**: Keeping `self@.inv()` on each function is a reasonable ergonomic
 choice — it saves callers from invoking invariant-preservation lemmas. The
 field-level unfoldings, however, add pure maintenance burden.
 
 ## Issues (highest priority first)
 
 1. **🔴 CRITICAL — `get` return value unspecified.** The ensures says
    `result is Some` on hit but never constrains what the `CacheGuard` provides.
    A conforming implementation could return any `V`. This defeats the fundamental
    purpose of the cache. The `spec_get` spec function computes the correct
    `Option<V>` but it is never connected to the exec return value.
 
 2. **🔴 CRITICAL — `CacheGuard::Deref`/`DerefMut` have no specs.** These are
    the only way callers access values from `get`. Without contracts, the
    specification chain from `put` → `get` → `*guard` is broken.
 
 3. **🟡 MODERATE — Pervasive subsumed clauses.** Every function carries 3–5
    ensures that merely unfold the canonical `== spec_*(…)` clause. This bloats
    the spec, increases maintenance burden, and risks divergence if spec functions
    are updated. Prune to `== spec_*(…)` + `inv()`.
 
 4. **🟡 MODERATE — Counter overflow unaddressed.** `u64` counter incremented
    without bounds checking. The property analysis identifies this (BUG-1) but
    it is not recorded in bugs.md or trust.md as a verification assumption.
 
 5. **🟢 MINOR — `inv()` redundant conjunct.** `lru_order.len() == contents.dom().len()`
    follows from `no_duplicates()` + `to_set() == dom()`. Acceptable as an SMT
    trigger / solver hint.
 
 6. **🟢 MINOR — No bugs.md file.** The property analysis identifies BUG-1
    (counter overflow) but no bugs.md exists to track it.
 
 ## Result: FAIL
 
 **Reason**: Two checklist items are unchecked:
 1. Subsumed ensures throughout all functions.
 2. `get` hit path does not meaningfully constrain the return value, and
    `CacheGuard::deref`/`deref_mut` lack specs entirely — callers cannot
    use the specification to verify correct data retrieval.
 
 Both CRITICAL issues (items 1–2) must be resolved before the specification

41. // CacheView - Abstract Specification Model
42. //==================================================================================================
43. 
44. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
45. ///
46. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
47. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
48. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
49. #[verifier::ext_equal]
50. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
51. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
52. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
53.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
54.     pub capacity: nat,
55.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
56. }
57. 
58. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
59. 
60.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
61.     // Well-formedness Invariant
62.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
63. 
64.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
65.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
66.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
67.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
68.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
69.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
70.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
71.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
72.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
73.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
74.     }
75. 
76.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
77.     // Helper Spec Functions
78.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
79. 
80.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
81.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
82.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
83.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
84.     }
85. 
86.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
87.     // Spec Transition Functions
88.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
89. 
90.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
91.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
92.         CacheView {
93.             contents: Map::empty(),
94.             capacity,
95.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
96.         }
97.     }
98. 
99.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
100.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
101.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
102.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
103.             (CacheView {
104.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
105.                 ..self
106.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
107.         } else {
108.             (self, None)
109.         }
110.     }
111. 
112.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
113.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
114.         if self.capacity == 0 {
115.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
116.             self
117.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
118.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
119.             CacheView {
120.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
121.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
122.                 ..self
123.             }
124.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
125.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
126.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
127.             CacheView {
128.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
129.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
130.                 ..self
131.             }
132.         } else {
133.             // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
134.             CacheView {
135.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
136.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
137.                 ..self
138.             }
139.         }
140.     }
141. 
142.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::remove`.
143.     pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
144.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
145.             CacheView {
146.                 contents: self.contents.remove(key),
147.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
148.                 ..self
149.             }
150.         } else {
151.             // Key absent: no-op.
152.             self
153.         }
154.     }
155. 
156.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::clear`.
157.     pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
158.         CacheView {
159.             contents: Map::empty(),
160.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
161.             ..self  // capacity preserved
162.         }
163.     }
164. }

171. // All constraints on the view come from the external_body method ensures clauses.
172. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> View for Cache<K, V> {
173.     type V = CacheView<K, V>;
174. 
175.     uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> CacheView<K, V>;
176. }

201.     ///
202.     /// # Parameters
203.     ///
204.     /// - `key`: The cache key to insert or update.
205.     /// - `value`: The value to store.
206.     ///
207.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
208.     #[verus_spec(
209.         requires
210.             old(self)@.inv(),
211.         ensures
212.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value),
213.             self@.inv(),
214.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
215.             // Put-get round-trip: if capacity > 0, the key is now present.
216.             old(self)@.capacity > 0 ==> {
217.                 &&& self@.contents.dom().contains(key)
218.                 &&& self@.contents[key] == value
219.             },
220.             // Zero-capacity no-op.
221.             old(self)@.capacity == 0 ==> self@ == old(self)@,
222.     )]
223.     pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
224.         // A zero-capacity cache cannot store entries.
225.         if self.capacity == 0 {
226.             return;
227.         }
228. 
229.         // If the key is already present, update in place.
230.         if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(&key) {
231.             self.counter += 1;
232.             entry.value = value;
233.             entry.last_used = self.counter;
234.             return;
235.         }
236. 
237.         // Evict the LRU entry if at capacity.
238.         if self.entries.len() >= self.capacity {
239.             self.evict();
240.         }
241. 
242.         self.counter += 1;
243.         self.entries.insert(
244.             key,
245.             CacheEntry {
246.                 value,
247.                 last_used: self.counter,
248.             },
249.         );
250.     }

253.     /// # Description
254.     ///
255.     /// Removes a specific key.
256.     ///
257.     /// # Parameters
258.     ///
259.     /// - `key`: The cache key to remove.
260.     ///

262.     #[verus_spec(
263.         requires
264.             old(self)@.inv(),
265.         ensures
266.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_remove(*key),
267.             self@.inv(),
268.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
269.             // Key is no longer present.
270.             !self@.contents.dom().contains(*key),
271.             // Key absent: no-op.
272.             !old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> self@ == old(self)@,
273.     )]
274.     pub fn remove(&mut self, key: &K) {
275.         self.entries.remove(key);
276.     }
277. 
278.     ///
279.     /// # Description
280.     ///
281.     /// Removes all entries.
282.     ///
283.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
284.     #[verus_spec(
285.         requires
286.             old(self)@.inv(),
287.         ensures
288.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_clear(),
289.             self@.inv(),
290.             self@.contents == Map::<K, V>::empty(),
291.             self@.lru_order == Seq::<K>::empty(),
292.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
293.     )]
294.     pub fn clear(&mut self) {
295.         self.entries.clear();
296.         self.counter = 0;
297.     }
298. 
299.     ///
300.     /// # Description
301.     ///
302.     /// Evicts the entry with the smallest `last_used` counter.
303.     ///
304.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
305.     #[verus_spec(
306.         requires
307.             old(self)@.inv(),
308.             old(self)@.contents.dom().len() > 0,
309.         ensures
310.             // The LRU victim (index 0) is evicted.
311.             !self@.contents.dom().contains(old(self)@.lru_order[0]),
312.             self@.contents == old(self)@.contents.remove(old(self)@.lru_order[0]),
313.             self@.contents.dom().len() == old(self)@.contents.dom().len() - 1,
314.             self@.lru_order == old(self)@.lru_order.subrange(1, old(self)@.lru_order.len() as int),
315.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
316.             self@.inv(),
317.     )]
318.     fn evict(&mut self) {
319.         let victim: Option<K> = self
320.             .entries
321.             .iter()
322.             .min_by_key(|(_, e)| e.last_used)
323.             .map(|(k, _)| k.clone());
324.         if let Some(key) = victim {
325.             self.entries.remove(&key);
326.         }
327.     }
328. }

100.

102. // Cache
103. //==================================================================================================
104. 
105. ///
106. /// # Description
107. ///
108. /// A bounded cache using access-counter LRU approximation.
109. ///
110. /// Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by `K`. A monotonic counter tracks access order;
111. /// on eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed. Lookups bump the
112. /// counter to mark the entry as recently used.
113. ///
114. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(K))]
115. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(V))]
116. pub struct Cache<K, V> {
117.     /// Cached entries.
118.     entries: BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
119.     /// Monotonically increasing counter for LRU ordering.
120.     counter: u64,
121.     /// Maximum number of entries.
122.     capacity: usize,
123. }

125. #[verus_verify]
126. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> Cache<K, V> {
127.     ///
128.     /// # Description
129.     ///
130.     /// Creates a new empty cache with the given capacity.
131.     ///
132.     /// # Parameters
133.     ///
134.     /// - `capacity`: Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
135.     ///
136.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
137.     #[verus_spec(result =>
138.         ensures
139.             result@ == CacheView::<K, V>::spec_new(capacity as nat),
140.             result@.inv(),
141.             result@.contents == Map::<K, V>::empty(),
142.             result@.capacity == capacity as nat,
143.             result@.lru_order == Seq::<K>::empty(),
144.     )]
145.     pub const fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
146.         Self {
147.             entries: BTreeMap::new(),
148.             counter: 0,
149.             capacity,
150.         }
151.     }
152.

### `Deref for CacheGuard<'_, V>`
- **Target:** `V`
- **Expected semantics:** `*guard` yields `&V` — an immutable reference to
  the cached value. The compiler inserts `deref()` for `*` and auto-deref
  coercions.

### `DerefMut for CacheGuard<'_, V>`
- **Expected semantics:** `*guard` yields `&mut V` — a mutable reference to
  the cached value, allowing in-place updates. The compiler inserts
  `deref_mut()` for `*` on `&mut` contexts.

### `Clone for CacheEntry<V>` (derived, private)
- Internal only. Required by `BTreeMap` iteration during eviction, which
  clones the victim key (`K: Clone`).

## Caller Expectations

### `Cache::new(capacity: usize) -> Self`
- **Callers assume:** Returns an empty cache that can hold up to `capacity`
  entries. Subsequent `get` on any key returns `None`. The cache is
  immediately usable.
- **Callers don't care about:** Internal counter initialization value, choice
  of backing data structure, or memory pre-allocation strategy.

### `Cache::get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<CacheGuard<'_, V>>`
- **Callers assume:**
  - Returns `Some(guard)` if the key is present, `None` otherwise.
  - The guard dereferences to the stored value (immutable or mutable access).
  - A successful `get` refreshes the entry's recency — the entry is no longer
    the LRU candidate (tests: `get_refreshes_lru_order`).
  - The cache size does not change.
  - The guard borrows the cache mutably; the caller cannot hold multiple
    guards or call other cache methods while a guard is live.
- **Callers don't care about:** The counter value, how recency is tracked
  internally, or the exact eviction ordering among entries with similar
  access patterns.

### `Cache::put(&mut self, key: K, value: V)`
- **Callers assume:**
  - **New key, below capacity:** the entry is inserted and immediately
    retrievable via `get`.
  - **New key, at capacity:** the least-recently-used entry is evicted first,
    then the new entry is inserted. Size stays at capacity
    (tests: `evicts_lru_entry_when_full`, `capacity_one`).
  - **Existing key (overwrite):** the value is replaced in-place; no eviction
    occurs; cache size does not change (tests: `put_overwrites_existing_key`,
    `overwrite_does_not_evict`).
  - **Zero-capacity cache:** `put` is a no-op (defensive guard in code).
--
### `CacheGuard::deref(&self) -> &V`
- **Callers assume:** Yields an immutable reference to the value that was
  stored in the cache. The reference is valid for the guard's lifetime.
- **Callers don't care about:** Guard internals.

### `CacheGuard::deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut V`
- **Callers assume:** Yields a mutable reference to the cached value,
  allowing in-place modification. Changes persist in the cache after the
  guard is dropped.
- **Callers don't care about:** Guard internals.

arguments.prompt:
I'm fixing Verus formal specifications for a bounded LRU cache module. A reviewer found issues. Here's my plan — please critique it.

## Context
- Cache uses BTreeMap (no vstd specs) — all methods are `external_body`
- CacheGuard has `value: &'a mut V` — Verus doesn't support `&mut` in struct fields
- CacheGuard is declared as `external_type_specification` + `external_body` (opaque to Verus)
- All spec transitions (`spec_new`, `spec_get`, etc.) are `pub open spec fn`

## Review Issues (from review_r1.md)

1. **🔴 CRITICAL — `get` return value unspecified**: `result is Some` on hit but no link to cached value. `spec_get` returns `(CacheView, Option<V>)` but the `Option<V>` is never referenced.

2. **🔴 CRITICAL — `CacheGuard::Deref`/`DerefMut` have no specs**: These are the only way callers extract values. Specification chain is broken.

3. **🟡 MODERATE — Subsumed ensures**: Every function has 3-5 ensures that just unfold the canonical `== spec_*()` clause. Since spec functions are `pub open`, these are redundant.

4. **🟡 MODERATE — Counter overflow unaddressed**: `u64` counter incremented without bounds check. Need bugs.md entry.

5. **🟢 MINOR — No bugs.md**: Need to create it.

## My Fix Plan

### Fix 1: Add View for CacheGuard + strengthen get ensures
Add to lib.spec.rs:
```rust
impl<'a, V> View for CacheGuard<'a, V> {
    type V = V;
    uninterp spec fn view(&self) -> V;
}
```
Then strengthen get's ensures on hit to include:
```rust
old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> {
    &&& result is Some
    &&& result->Some_0@ == old(self)@.contents[*key]
    &&& self@ == old(self)@.spec_get(*key).0
    &&& self@.inv()
},
```
This connects the return value to the cached value through the CacheGuard's View.

### Fix 2: Add Deref spec
Add `#[verus_verify]` to the `impl Deref for CacheGuard` block and add:
```rust
#[verus_verify(external_body)]
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    ensures *ret == self@,
)]
fn deref(&self) -> &V {
    self.value
}
```
This says dereferencing the returned `&V` gives you the View of the guard.

### Fix 3: Add DerefMut spec (attempt, may fail)
Try adding spec to `deref_mut`. Since it returns `&mut V`, Verus might reject it. If it fails, document the limitation in trust.md but don't try to workaround.

### Fix 4: Prune subsumed ensures
For each function, keep only:
- Canonical transition: `self@ == old(self)@.spec_X(args)` (or `result@ == ...` for new)
- Invariant preservation: `self@.inv()`
Remove all field-level unfoldings.

### Fix 5: Create bugs.md for counter overflow
Record BUG-1: counter overflow when `u64` counter wraps.

### Fix 6: Update trust.md
Add counter overflow assumption and DerefMut limitation (if Fix 3 fails).

## Concerns

1. Will `result->Some_0@` work? This accesses the 0th field of `Option::Some` variant, then calls View on CacheGuard. CacheGuard has external_type_specification + external_body, so View should work.

2. Will `*ret == self@` work in the Deref spec? `*ret` is `V` (dereferencing `&V`), and `self@` is `V` (View of CacheGuard). Both are `V`, so equality should work. But `*ret` in a spec context — does Verus support dereferencing a reference in specs?

3. For the Deref impl block — can I add `#[verus_verify]` on an impl block for a type that was declared with `external_type_specification`?

Please critique this plan, especially concerns 1-3 and any issues I'm missing.

---
name: review-methodology
description: "Review Verus verification code with focus on spec quality and automated checks."
---

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code (use `detect_cheating` tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

43. 
44. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
45. ///
46. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
47. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
48. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
49. #[verifier::ext_equal]
50. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
51. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
52. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
53.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
54.     pub capacity: nat,
55.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
56. }
57. 
58. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
59. 
60.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
61.     // Well-formedness Invariant
62.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
63. 
64.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
65.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
66.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
67.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
68.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
69.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
70.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
71.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
72.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
73.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
74.     }
75. 
76.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
77.     // Helper Spec Functions
78.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
79. 
80.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
81.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
82.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
83.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
84.     }
85. 
86.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
87.     // Spec Transition Functions
88.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
89. 
90.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
91.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
92.         CacheView {
93.             contents: Map::empty(),
94.             capacity,
95.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
96.         }
97.     }
98. 
99.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
100.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
101.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
102.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
103.             (CacheView {
104.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
105.                 ..self
106.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
107.         } else {
108.             (self, None)
109.         }
110.     }
111. 
112.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
113.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
114.         if self.capacity == 0 {
115.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
116.             self
117.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
118.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
119.             CacheView {
120.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
121.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
122.                 ..self
123.             }
124.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
125.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
126.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
127.             CacheView {
128.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
129.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
130.                 ..self
131.             }
132.         } else {
133.             // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
134.             CacheView {
135.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
136.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
137.                 ..self
138.             }
139.         }
140.     }
141. 
142.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::remove`.
143.     pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
144.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
145.             CacheView {
146.                 contents: self.contents.remove(key),
147.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
148.                 ..self
149.             }
150.         } else {
151.             // Key absent: no-op.
152.             self
153.         }
154.     }
155. 
156.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::clear`.
157.     pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
158.         CacheView {
159.             contents: Map::empty(),
160.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
161.             ..self  // capacity preserved
162.         }
163.     }
164. }

4. //! Bounded LRU cache backed by `BTreeMap`.
5. //!
6. //! Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by a caller-chosen type `K` that
7. //! implements `Ord + Clone`. A monotonic counter tracks access order; on
8. //! eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed.
9. //! Lookups bump the counter to mark the entry as recently used.
10. //!
11. //! # Capacity
12. //!
13. //! The cache is bounded by a capacity given at construction time. When the
14. //! cache is full, the least-recently-used entry is evicted before inserting a
15. //! new one.
16. //!
17. //! # Example
18. //!
19. //! ```
20. //! use cache::Cache;
21. //!
22. //! let mut cache: Cache<&str, i32> = Cache::new(2);
23. //! cache.put("a", 1);
24. //! cache.put("b", 2);
25. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"a").unwrap(), 1);
26. //!
27. //! // Inserting a third entry evicts "b" (least recently used).
28. //! cache.put("c", 3);
29. //! assert!(cache.get(&"b").is_none());
30. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"c").unwrap(), 3);
31. //! ```

105. ///
106. /// # Description
107. ///
108. /// A bounded cache using access-counter LRU approximation.
109. ///
110. /// Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by `K`. A monotonic counter tracks access order;
111. /// on eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed. Lookups bump the
112. /// counter to mark the entry as recently used.
113. ///
114. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(K))]
115. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(V))]
116. pub struct Cache<K, V> {
117.     /// Cached entries.
118.     entries: BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
119.     /// Monotonically increasing counter for LRU ordering.
120.     counter: u64,
121.     /// Maximum number of entries.
122.     capacity: usize,
123. }
124. 
125. #[verus_verify]
126. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> Cache<K, V> {
127.     ///
128.     /// # Description
129.     ///
130.     /// Creates a new empty cache with the given capacity.
131.     ///
132.     /// # Parameters
133.     ///
134.     /// - `capacity`: Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
135.     ///
136.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
137.     #[verus_spec(result =>
138.         ensures
139.             result@ == CacheView::<K, V>::spec_new(capacity as nat),
140.             result@.inv(),
141.             result@.contents == Map::<K, V>::empty(),
142.             result@.capacity == capacity as nat,
143.             result@.lru_order == Seq::<K>::empty(),
144.     )]
145.     pub const fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
146.         Self {
147.             entries: BTreeMap::new(),
148.             counter: 0,
149.             capacity,
150.         }
151.     }
152. 
153.     ///
154.     /// # Description
155.     ///
156.     /// Looks up a cached value and bumps its LRU counter on hit.
157.     ///
158.     /// # Parameters
159.     ///
160.     /// - `key`: The cache key to look up.
161.     ///
162.     /// # Returns
163.     ///
164.     /// An RAII guard providing access to the cached value, or `None` on cache miss.
165.     ///
166.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
167.     #[verus_spec(result =>
168.         requires
169.             old(self)@.inv(),
170.         ensures
171.             // Hit: key is present.
172.             old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> {
173.                 &&& result is Some
174.                 &&& self@ == old(self)@.spec_get(*key).0
175.                 &&& self@.contents == old(self)@.contents
176.                 &&& self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity
177.                 &&& self@.inv()
178.             },
179.             // Miss: key is absent.
180.             !old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> {
181.                 &&& result is None
182.                 &&& self@ == old(self)@
183.             },
184.     )]
185.     pub fn get(&mut self, key: &K) -> Option<CacheGuard<'_, V>> {
186.         if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(key) {
187.             self.counter += 1;
188.             entry.last_used = self.counter;
189.             Some(CacheGuard {
190.                 value: &mut entry.value,
191.             })
192.         } else {
193.             None
194.         }
195.     }
196. 
197.     ///
198.     /// # Description
199.     ///
200.     /// Inserts a value, evicting the least-recently-used entry if at capacity.
201.     ///
202.     /// # Parameters
203.     ///
204.     /// - `key`: The cache key to insert or update.
205.     /// - `value`: The value to store.
206.     ///
207.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
208.     #[verus_spec(
209.         requires
210.             old(self)@.inv(),
211.         ensures
212.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value),
213.             self@.inv(),
214.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
215.             // Put-get round-trip: if capacity > 0, the key is now present.
216.             old(self)@.capacity > 0 ==> {
217.                 &&& self@.contents.dom().contains(key)
218.                 &&& self@.contents[key] == value
219.             },
220.             // Zero-capacity no-op.
221.             old(self)@.capacity == 0 ==> self@ == old(self)@,
222.     )]
223.     pub fn put(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
224.         // A zero-capacity cache cannot store entries.
225.         if self.capacity == 0 {
226.             return;
227.         }
228. 
229.         // If the key is already present, update in place.
230.         if let Some(entry) = self.entries.get_mut(&key) {
231.             self.counter += 1;
232.             entry.value = value;
233.             entry.last_used = self.counter;
234.             return;
235.         }
236. 
237.         // Evict the LRU entry if at capacity.
238.         if self.entries.len() >= self.capacity {
239.             self.evict();
240.         }
241. 
242.         self.counter += 1;
243.         self.entries.insert(
244.             key,
245.             CacheEntry {
246.                 value,
247.                 last_used: self.counter,
248.             },
249.         );
250.     }
251. 
252.     ///
253.     /// # Description
254.     ///
255.     /// Removes a specific key.
256.     ///
257.     /// # Parameters
258.     ///
259.     /// - `key`: The cache key to remove.
260.     ///
261.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
262.     #[verus_spec(
263.         requires
264.             old(self)@.inv(),
265.         ensures
266.             self@ == old(self)@.spec_remove(*key),
267.             self@.inv(),
268.             self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity,
269.             // Key is no longer present.
270.             !self@.contents.dom().contains(*key),
271.             // Key absent: no-op.
272.             !old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> self@ == old(self)@,
273.     )]
274.     pub fn remove(&mut self, key: &K) {
275.         self.entries.remove(key);
276.     }

6. ## Root Cause
7. 
8. `BTreeMap` (from `alloc::collections`) has no vstd specifications — no View trait,
9. no `assume_specification` for any method (`new`, `get_mut`, `insert`, `remove`, `clear`,
10. `len`, `iter`, `min_by_key`). This makes body verification of any Cache method impossible.
11. All methods are marked `external_body` with comprehensive pre/post conditions.
12. 
13. Additionally, `CacheGuard` contains `&'a mut V` which Verus cannot handle in struct
14. fields ("The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases").

22.   declaration to reference it in verified structs. `external_body` is needed because
23.   BTreeMap has private fields.

25.   "cannot use type `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` which is ignored because it is either

1. # Specification Review: cache
2. 
3. > Consolidated from independent reviews by claude-opus-4.6 and gpt-5.3-codex.
4. > Raw outputs: `review_r1.claude.md`, `review_r1.gpt.md`.
5. 
6. ## Checklist
7. ### Specification
8. - [x] Every in-scope exec function has requires/ensures
9. - [x] No tautological ensures (e.g., `Err(_) => true`)
10. - [ ] No subsumed ensures (derivable from inv() + other ensures)
11. - [ ] Error paths have meaningful ensures (match style: Ok => ..., Err => ...)
12. - [x] No assume_specification for workspace-internal code
13. - [x] vstd searched before any assume_specification
14. - [ ] Specs written for the caller (usable directly in caller proofs)
15. 
16. **Unchecked items:**
17. - **Subsumed ensures**: Every function (`new`, `get`, `put`, `remove`, `clear`)
18.   carries 3–5 ensures clauses that are strict unfoldings of the `== spec_*(…)`
19.   canonical clause. Since all spec transition functions are `pub open spec fn`,
20.   callers can unfold them directly. These clauses are redundant bloat.
21. - **Error paths**: `get` on miss is well-specified (`self@ == old(self)@`), but
22.   the hit path does not meaningfully constrain the return value — `result is Some`
23.   without any link to the cached value is effectively a one-sided spec.
24. - **Caller usability**: `CacheGuard::deref` and `CacheGuard::deref_mut` have
25.   **no specs at all**. Since these are the only way callers extract values from
26.   `get`, the specification chain is broken: callers cannot prove they receive
27.   the correct value.
28. 
29. ## Determinism Check
30. | Function | Result | Under-constrained aspect |
31. |---|---|---|
32. | `Cache::get` (return value) | INCOMPLETE | On hit: only `result is Some`. The value inside `CacheGuard` is entirely unconstrained — no View impl, no Deref spec. A conforming implementation could return arbitrary data. |
33. | `CacheGuard::deref` | INCOMPLETE | No spec at all. |
34. | `CacheGuard::deref_mut` | INCOMPLETE | No spec at all. |
35. 
36. All other functions (`new`, `put`, `remove`, `clear`, `evict`) are COMPLETE —
37. the `== spec_*(…)` clause fully determines the post-state and return value.
38. 
39. ## Caller Coverage Issues
40. | Function | Status | Notes |
41. |---|---|---|
42. | `Cache::get` | MISSING_SPEC | Return value unconstrained on hit. Caller expectation "guard dereferences to stored value" (caller analysis §CacheGuard::deref) is unverifiable. |
43. | `CacheGuard::deref` | MISSING_SPEC | No contract. This is the primary value-extraction interface. |
44. | `CacheGuard::deref_mut` | MISSING_SPEC | No contract. Mutation-through-guard behavior unmodeled. |
45. | `Cache::new` | SUBSUMED | 4 ensures clauses are unfoldings of `spec_new` (which is `open`). |
46. | `Cache::put` | SUBSUMED | Round-trip and zero-cap clauses derivable from `spec_put`. |
47. | `Cache::remove` | SUBSUMED | Key-absent no-op and key-not-present clauses derivable from `spec_remove`. |
48. | `Cache::clear` | SUBSUMED | Emptiness/order/capacity clauses derivable from `spec_clear`. |
49. 
50. ## Missing Properties
51. 1. **Get-value correctness (CRITICAL)** — The fundamental cache contract ("you
52.    get back what you put in") is unverifiable. `get` on hit says `result is Some`
53.    but never connects the `CacheGuard` to `old(self)@.contents[*key]`. The
54.    `spec_get` transition function returns `(CacheView, Option<V>)` and the
55.    `Option<V>` component is never referenced in the exec ensures.
56.    **Fix**: Either (a) add a View impl for `CacheGuard` mapping to `V` plus a
57.    spec on `Deref`, or (b) add an ensures clause directly on `get` such as
58.    `result matches Some(g) ==> *g == old(self)@.contents[*key]` (if Verus can
59.    express this through the external-body guard).
60. 
61. 2. **Guard mutation effect** — If a caller mutates through `DerefMut`, the
62.    cache entry should reflect the change. Currently unspecified. This is a
63.    known Verus limitation (`&mut` in struct fields) but should be documented
64.    in trust.md.
65. 
66. 3. **Counter overflow** — `self.counter` is `u64`, incremented on every `get`
67.    hit and `put`. The spec has no precondition guarding overflow. While 2⁶⁴
68.    operations is physically unreachable, a rigorous spec would either add
69.    `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` or document the trust assumption. The
70.    property analysis (BUG-1) identifies this; it should be recorded in
71.    trust.md.
72. 
73. ## Specs to Remove
74. - **`new`**: Remove `result@.inv()`, `result@.contents == Map::empty()`,
75.   `result@.capacity == capacity as nat`, `result@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`.
76.   All derivable from `result@ == spec_new(…)` (open spec).
77. - **`get` (hit)**: Remove `self@.contents == old(self)@.contents`,
78.   `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, `self@.inv()`.
79.   All derivable from `self@ == old(self)@.spec_get(*key).0`.
80. - **`put`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`, put-get round-trip
81.   block, zero-capacity no-op block. All derivable from `self@ == spec_put(…)`.
82. - **`remove`**: Remove `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`,
83.   `!self@.contents.dom().contains(*key)`,
84.   `!old(self)@.contents.dom().contains(*key) ==> self@ == old(self)@`.
85.   All derivable from `self@ == spec_remove(…)`.
86. - **`clear`**: Remove `self@.contents == Map::empty()`,
87.   `self@.lru_order == Seq::empty()`, `self@.capacity == old(self)@.capacity`.
88.   All derivable from `self@ == spec_clear()`.
89. 
90. **Caveat**: Keeping `self@.inv()` on each function is a reasonable ergonomic
91. choice — it saves callers from invoking invariant-preservation lemmas. The
92. field-level unfoldings, however, add pure maintenance burden.
93. 
94. ## Issues (highest priority first)
95. 
96. 1. **🔴 CRITICAL — `get` return value unspecified.** The ensures says
97.    `result is Some` on hit but never constrains what the `CacheGuard` provides.
98.    A conforming implementation could return any `V`. This defeats the fundamental
99.    purpose of the cache. The `spec_get` spec function computes the correct
100.    `Option<V>` but it is never connected to the exec return value.
101. 
102. 2. **🔴 CRITICAL — `CacheGuard::Deref`/`DerefMut` have no specs.** These are
103.    the only way callers access values from `get`. Without contracts, the
104.    specification chain from `put` → `get` → `*guard` is broken.
105. 
106. 3. **🟡 MODERATE — Pervasive subsumed clauses.** Every function carries 3–5
107.    ensures that merely unfold the canonical `== spec_*(…)` clause. This bloats
108.    the spec, increases maintenance burden, and risks divergence if spec functions
109.    are updated. Prune to `== spec_*(…)` + `inv()`.
110. 
111. 4. **🟡 MODERATE — Counter overflow unaddressed.** `u64` counter incremented
112.    without bounds checking. The property analysis identifies this (BUG-1) but
113.    it is not recorded in bugs.md or trust.md as a verification assumption.
114. 
115. 5. **🟢 MINOR — `inv()` redundant conjunct.** `lru_order.len() == contents.dom().len()`
116.    follows from `no_duplicates()` + `to_set() == dom()`. Acceptable as an SMT
117.    trigger / solver hint.
118. 
119. 6. **🟢 MINOR — No bugs.md file.** The property analysis identifies BUG-1
120.    (counter overflow) but no bugs.md exists to track it.
121. 
122. ## Result: FAIL
123. 
124. **Reason**: Two checklist items are unchecked:
125. 1. Subsumed ensures throughout all functions.
126. 2. `get` hit path does not meaningfully constrain the return value, and
127.    `CacheGuard::deref`/`deref_mut` lack specs entirely — callers cannot
128.    use the specification to verify correct data retrieval.
129. 
130. Both CRITICAL issues (items 1–2) must be resolved before the specification
131. can pass review.
132.

{"type":"output_text","text":{"value":"In Verus, for a function that returns a reference `&T`, **the postcondition is usually written as `*result == ...` rather than `result@ == ...`**.

### Explanation

- `result@` (pronounced as "result at-ghost") gives you the **value** encoded by a returned type, but only if the return type is something that has an associated "ghost" representation, such as types marked with `Tracked` or `Ghost`. Regular references like `&T` are **not** ghost types, so `result@` does not give you the referenced value for `&T`.
- To refer to the value **pointed to** by a reference, you dereference it: `*result`.
- So, for a function that returns `&T`, in its postcondition (ensures), you write `*result == ...` to specify a property about the value pointed to by the returned reference.

#### Example

```rust
fn max_ref(a: &int, b: &int) -> &int
    ensures
        *result == if *a >= *b { *a } else { *b }
{
    if *a >= *b { a } else { b }
}
```

Here, `*result == ...` is the correct way to write the postcondition.

#### When would you use `result@`?

You use `result@` **only** when the return type is a tracked/ghost value, for example:

```rust
fn foo(x: Tracked<int>) -> Tracked<int>
    ensures result@ == x@ + 1
{ ... }
```

But for references (`&T`), **use `*result` in the ensures clause**.

---

**Summary:**  
For functions returning `&T`, the postcondition uses `*result`, not `result@`.","annotations":null},"bing_searches":null,"annotations":null}

### Explanation

- `result@` (pronounced as "result at-ghost") gives you the **value** encoded by a returned type, but only if the return type is something that has an associated "ghost" representation, such as types marked with `Tracked` or `Ghost`. Regular references like `&T` are **not** ghost types, so `result@` does not give you the referenced value for `&T`.
- To refer to the value **pointed to** by a reference, you dereference it: `*result`.
- So, for a function that returns `&T`, in its postcondition (ensures), you write `*result == ...` to specify a property about the value pointed to by the returned reference.

#### Example

```rust
fn max_ref(a: &int, b: &int) -> &int
    ensures
        *result == if *a >= *b { *a } else { *b }
{
    if *a >= *b { a } else { b }
}
```

Here, `*result == ...` is the correct way to write the postcondition.

#### When would you use `result@`?

You use `result@` **only** when the return type is a tracked/ghost value, for example:

```rust
fn foo(x: Tracked<int>) -> Tracked<int>
    ensures result@ == x@ + 1
{ ... }
```

But for references (`&T`), **use `*result` in the ensures clause**.

---

8. ## Ghost/Tracked Parameters (`with` clause)
9. 
10. Functions can accept ghost/tracked parameters invisible to non-Verus callers.
11. 
12. ### Declaring a function with ghost/tracked params
13. 
14. ```rust
15. #[verus_spec(ret =>
16.     with
17.         Tracked(y): Tracked<&mut u32>,
18.         Ghost(w): Ghost<u64>
19.             -> z: Ghost<u32>
20.     requires
21.         x < 100,
22.         *old(y) < 100,
23.     ensures
24.         *y == x,
25.         ret == x,
26.         z == x,
27. )]
28. fn test_mut_tracked(x: u32) -> u32 {
29.     proof!{ *y = x; }
30.     #[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]
31.     x
32. }
33. ```
34. 
35. - The `with` clause declares ghost/tracked inputs and ghost outputs (`-> z: Ghost<u32>`).
36. - `#[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]` on the return expression returns a ghost output.
37. 
38. ### Calling with ghost/tracked
39. 
40. Use `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` on the call expression:
41. 
42. ```rust
43. fn test_cal_mut_tracked(x: u32) {
44.     proof_decl!{
45.         let ghost mut z;
46.         let tracked mut y = 0u32;
47.         z = 0u32;
48.     }
49. 
50.     // On a let statement:
51.     #[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0) => Ghost(z))]
52.     let _ = test_mut_tracked(0u32);
53. 
54.     // On a bare expression (wrap in parens):
55.     (#[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0))]
56.     test_mut_tracked(0u32));
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. ### How it works
61. 
62. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` generates **two versions** of the function:
63. - A verified version (`_VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`) with ghost/tracked parameters
64. - An unverified version (original signature) with `requires false`
65. 
66. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` at the call site calls the verified version.
67. Without it, the unverified version is called — which has `requires false`,
68. so calling from verified code without the `with` annotation will fail.
69. 
70. Unverified code can call the original version normally:
71. 
72. ```rust
73. fn external_caller(x: u32) -> u32 {
74.     test_mut_tracked(1)  // calls unverified version, no with needed
75. }
76. ```

79. 
80. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` call-site syntax only works with exec functions
81. verified via `#[verus_spec]`. Using it to call an exec function defined
82. inside `verus! { }` will error: `cannot find function _VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`.

88. #[verus_spec(v =>
89.     with Tracked(perm): Tracked<&mut PointsTo<T>>
90.     requires
91.         old(perm).ptr() == ptr,
92.         old(perm).is_init(),
93.     ensures
94.         perm.ptr() == ptr,
95.         perm.is_uninit(),
96.         v == old(perm).value(),
97. )]
98. fn ptr_mut_read<'a, T>(ptr: *const T) -> T {
99.     vstd::raw_ptr::ptr_mut_read(ptr, Tracked::assume_new())
100. }
101. ```

112.     requires x < 100, y < 100,
113.     returns add(x, y),
114. )]
115. fn add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
116.     proof! { assert(true); }

118. }
119. // Generates: spec fn spec_add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 { x + y }
120. // Proof/ghost code is stripped from the generated spec function

130.     returns f2(x),
131. )]
132. pub fn f2(x: u32) -> u32 {
133.     add(x, 1)
134. }
135. // Use f2(x) directly in spec context — resolves to __VERUS_SPEC_f2(x)
136. ```
137. 
138. Works on impl methods too:
139. 
140. ```rust
141. impl S {
142.     #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
143.     #[verus_spec(
144.         returns self.foo(x),
145.     )]
146.     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32 { x }
147. }

164.             0 <= i < 10,
165.             0 <= j < 10,
166.         ensures

169.     )]

 # Verus Attribute Syntax — Advanced Guide
 
 Companion to `SKILL.md`. Covers patterns needed less frequently.
 See also `syntax_attr.rs` in this directory for the official Verus example.
 
 ---
 
 ## Ghost/Tracked Parameters (`with` clause)
 
 Functions can accept ghost/tracked parameters invisible to non-Verus callers.
 
 ### Declaring a function with ghost/tracked params
 
 ```rust
 #[verus_spec(ret =>
     with
         Tracked(y): Tracked<&mut u32>,
         Ghost(w): Ghost<u64>
             -> z: Ghost<u32>
     requires
         x < 100,
         *old(y) < 100,
     ensures
         *y == x,
         ret == x,
         z == x,
 )]
 fn test_mut_tracked(x: u32) -> u32 {
     proof!{ *y = x; }
     #[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]
     x
 }
 ```
 
 - The `with` clause declares ghost/tracked inputs and ghost outputs (`-> z: Ghost<u32>`).
 - `#[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]` on the return expression returns a ghost output.
 
 ### Calling with ghost/tracked
 
 Use `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` on the call expression:
 
 ```rust
 fn test_cal_mut_tracked(x: u32) {
     proof_decl!{
         let ghost mut z;
         let tracked mut y = 0u32;
         z = 0u32;
     }
 
     // On a let statement:
     #[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0) => Ghost(z))]
     let _ = test_mut_tracked(0u32);
 
     // On a bare expression (wrap in parens):
     (#[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0))]
     test_mut_tracked(0u32));
 }
 ```
 
 ### How it works
 
 `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` generates **two versions** of the function:
 - A verified version (`_VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`) with ghost/tracked parameters
 - An unverified version (original signature) with `requires false`
 
 `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` at the call site calls the verified version.
 Without it, the unverified version is called — which has `requires false`,
 so calling from verified code without the `with` annotation will fail.
 
 Unverified code can call the original version normally:
 
 ```rust
 fn external_caller(x: u32) -> u32 {
     test_mut_tracked(1)  // calls unverified version, no with needed
 }
 ```
 
 ### Compatibility limitation
 
 `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` call-site syntax only works with exec functions
 verified via `#[verus_spec]`. Using it to call an exec function defined
 inside `verus! { }` will error: `cannot find function _VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`.
 
 Workaround: create a trusted wrapper:
 
 ```rust
 #[verus_verify(external_body)]
 #[verus_spec(v =>
     with Tracked(perm): Tracked<&mut PointsTo<T>>
     requires
         old(perm).ptr() == ptr,
         old(perm).is_init(),
     ensures
         perm.ptr() == ptr,
         perm.is_uninit(),
         v == old(perm).value(),
 )]
 fn ptr_mut_read<'a, T>(ptr: *const T) -> T {
     vstd::raw_ptr::ptr_mut_read(ptr, Tracked::assume_new())
 }
 ```
 
 ---
 
 ## Dual-Mode Functions (exec → spec)
 
 Automatically generate a spec mirror of an exec function:
 
 ```rust
 #[verus_verify(dual_spec(spec_add))]
 #[verus_spec(
     requires x < 100, y < 100,
     returns add(x, y),
 )]
 fn add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
     proof! { assert(true); }
     x + y
 }
 // Generates: spec fn spec_add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 { x + y }
 // Proof/ghost code is stripped from the generated spec function
 ```
 
 Without a custom name, an internal name `__VERUS_SPEC_xxx` is generated.
 The `#[when_used_as_spec]` attribute lets you use the exec name as a spec:
 
 ```rust
 #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
 #[verus_spec(
     requires x < 100,
     returns f2(x),
 )]
 pub fn f2(x: u32) -> u32 {
     add(x, 1)
 }
 // Use f2(x) directly in spec context — resolves to __VERUS_SPEC_f2(x)
 ```
 
 Works on impl methods too:
 
 ```rust
 impl S {
     #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
     #[verus_spec(
         returns self.foo(x),
     )]
     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32 { x }
 }
 ```
 
 **Limitations:**
 - Requires `#[verus_spec]` — does not work with `verus!` macro
 - `&mut` parameters are not supported (spec functions cannot take `&mut`)
 - Not supported on trait implementations (error: "method `spec_f` is not
   a member of trait")
 
 ---
 
 ## Trait Function Specs
 
 ```rust
 trait MyTrait {
     #[verus_spec(r =>
         requires
             0 <= i < 10,
             0 <= j < 10,
         ensures
             i <= r,
             j <= r,
     )]
     fn compute(&self, i: u8, j: u8) -> u8;
 }
 ```
 
 Default trait implementations:
 
 ```rust
 #[verus_verify]
 trait SomeTrait {
     #[verus_spec(ret =>
         requires true,
         ensures ret,
     )]
     fn f(&self) -> bool {
         true
     }
 }
 ```
 
 **Limitation:** `with` (ghost/tracked parameters) is not supported on
 trait methods — error: "`with` does not support trait".
 
 ---
 
 ## Closure Specs
 
 ```rust
 let f =
     #[verus_spec(z: u64 =>
         requires y == 2,
         ensures z == 2,
     )]
     |y: u64| { y };
 
 proof! {
     assert(f.requires((2,)));
     assert(!f.ensures((2,), 3));
 }
 let t = f(2);
 proof! { assert(t == 2); }
 ```
 
 **Note:** Closures must have a return type annotation or a named return
 in the spec. A closure with no return type and no named return will error:
 "Closure must have a return type". Use either `|y: u64| -> () { }` or
 `#[verus_spec(ret: () => ...)]`.
 
 ---

1. // Official Verus attribute-syntax example
2. // Source: verus-lang/verus examples/syntax_attr.rs (commit 8d75ec4)
3. // This file is a reference copy — see the Verus repo for the latest version.
4. 
5. #![feature(proc_macro_hygiene)]
6. #![allow(unused_imports)]
7. 
8. use verus_builtin::*;
9. use verus_builtin_macros::*;
10. use vstd::{modes::*, prelude::*, seq::*, *};
11. 
12. fn main() {}
13. 
14. /// functions may be declared exec (default), proof, or spec, which contain
15. /// exec code, proof code, and spec code, respectively.
16. ///   - exec code: compiled, may have requires/ensures
17. ///   - proof code: erased before compilation, may have requires/ensures
18. ///   - spec code: erased before compilation, no requires/ensures, but may have recommends
19. /// exec and proof functions may name their return values inside parentheses, before the return type
20. #[verus_spec(sum =>
21.     requires
22.         x < 100,
23.         y < 100,
24.     ensures
25.         sum < 200,
26. )]
27. fn my_exec_fun(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32
28. {
29.     x + y
30. }
31. 
32. verus! {
33. 
34. proof fn my_proof_fun(x: int, y: int) -> (sum: int)
35.     requires
36.         x < 100,
37.         y < 100,
38.     ensures
39.         sum < 200,
40. {
41.     x + y
42. }
43. 
44. spec fn my_spec_fun(x: int, y: int) -> int
45.     recommends
46.         x < 100,
47.         y < 100,
48. {
49.     x + y
50. }
51. 
52. } // verus!
53. 
54. /// exec code cannot directly call proof functions or spec functions.
55. /// However, exec code can contain proof blocks (proof { ... }),
56. /// which contain proof code.
57. /// This proof code can call proof functions and spec functions.
58. #[verus_spec(
59.     requires
60.         x < 100,
61.         y < 100,
62. )]
63. fn test_my_funs(x: u32, y: u32)
64. {
65.     // my_proof_fun(x, y); // not allowed in exec code
66.     // let u = my_spec_fun(x, y); // not allowed exec code
67.     proof! {
68.         let u = my_spec_fun(x as int, y as int);  // allowed in proof code
69.         my_proof_fun(u / 2, y as int);  // allowed in proof code
70.     }
71. }
72. 
73. verus! {
74. 
75. /// spec functions with pub or pub(...) must specify whether the body of the function
76. /// should also be made publicly visible (open function) or not visible (closed function).
77. pub open spec fn my_pub_spec_fun1(x: int, y: int) -> int {
78.     // function and body visible to all
79.     x / 2 + y / 2
80. }
81. 
82. pub closed spec fn my_pub_spec_fun4(x: int, y: int) -> int {
83.     // function visible to all, body visible to module
84.     x / 2 + y / 2
85. }
86. 
87. pub(crate) closed spec fn my_pub_spec_fun5(x: int, y: int) -> int {
88.     // function visible to crate, body visible to module
89.     x / 2 + y / 2
90. }
91. 
92. } // verus!
93. 
94. /// Recursive functions must have decreases clauses so that Verus can verify that the functions
95. /// terminate.
96. #[verus_spec(
97.     requires
98.         0 < x < 100,
99.         y < 100 - x,
100.     decreases x,
101. )]
102. fn test_rec(x: u64, y: u64)
103. {
104.     if x > 1 {
105.         test_rec(x - 1, y + 1);
106.     }
107. }
108. 
109. verus! {
110. 
111. /// Multiple decreases clauses are ordered lexicographically, so that later clauses may
112. /// increase when earlier clauses decrease.
113. spec fn test_rec2(x: int, y: int) -> int
114.     decreases x, y,
115. {
116.     if y > 0 {
117.         1 + test_rec2(x, y - 1)
118.     } else if x > 0 {
119.         2 + test_rec2(x - 1, 100)
120.     } else {
121.         3
122.     }
123. }
124. 
125. /// To help prove termination, recursive spec functions may have embedded proof blocks
126. /// that can make assertions, use broadcasts, and call lemmas.
127. spec fn test_rec_proof_block(x: int, y: int) -> int
128.     decreases x,
129. {
130.     if x < 1 {
131.         0
132.     } else {
133.         proof {
134.             assert(x - 1 >= 0);
135.         }
136.         test_rec_proof_block(x - 1, y + 1) + 1
137.     }
138. }
139. 
140. /// Decreases and recommends may specify additional clauses:
141. ///   - decreases .. "when" restricts the function definition to a condition
142. ///     that makes the function terminate
143. ///   - decreases .. "via" specifies a proof function that proves the termination
144. ///   - recommends .. "when" specifies a proof function that proves the
145. ///     recommendations of the functions invoked in the body
146. spec fn add0(a: nat, b: nat) -> nat
147.     recommends
148.         a > 0,
149.     via add0_recommends
150. {
151.     a + b
152. }
153. 
154. spec fn dec0(a: int) -> int
155.     decreases a,
156.     when a > 0
157.     via dec0_decreases
158. {
159.     if a > 0 {
160.         dec0(a - 1)
161.     } else {
162.         0
163.     }
164. }
165. 
166. #[via_fn]
167. proof fn add0_recommends(a: nat, b: nat) {
168.     // proof
169. }
170. 
171. #[via_fn]
172. proof fn dec0_decreases(a: int) {
173.     // proof
174. }
175. 
176. } // verus!
177. 
178. /// variables may be exec, tracked, or ghost
179. ///   - exec: compiled
180. ///   - tracked: erased before compilation, checked for lifetimes (advanced feature)
181. ///   - ghost: erased before compilation, no lifetime checking
182. /// Different variable modes may be used in different code modes:
183. ///   - variables in exec code are always exec
184. ///   - variables in proof code are ghost by default (tracked variables must be marked "tracked")
185. ///   - variables in spec code are always ghost
186. #[verus_spec(
187.     requires
188.         a < 100,
189.         b < 100,
190. )]
191. fn test_my_funs2(
192.     a: u32,  // exec variable
193.     b: u32,  // exec variable
194. )
195. {
196.     let s = a + b;  // s is an exec variable
197.     proof! {
198.         let u = a + b;  // u is a ghost variable
199.         my_proof_fun(u / 2, b as int);  // my_proof_fun(x, y) takes ghost parameters x and y
200.     }
201. }

206. /// "assert by" may be used to provide proof code that proves the assertion.
207. #[verifier::opaque]
208. spec fn f1(i: int) -> int {

215. fn assert_by_test() {
216.     proof! {
217.         assert(f1(3) > 3) by {
218.             reveal(f1);  // reveal f1's definition just inside this block
219.         }
220.         assert(f1(3) > 3);
